content: 1. The second global survey on eHealth, conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO), was accessed on November 26, 2018. This survey provides insights into the global adoption and implementation of eHealth technologies. 2. Wootton R. explored the role of telemedicine in supporting healthcare delivery in developing countries, as published in the Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare in 2008. The study highlights the potential of telemedicine to address healthcare disparities in resource-limited settings. 3. Hersh WR, Hickam DH, Severance SM, Dana TL, Krages KP, and Helfand M. updated their evidence report on the use of telemedicine for the Medicare population in 2006. This report evaluates the effectiveness and feasibility of telemedicine interventions for older adults. 4. WHO guidelines on digital health interventions for strengthening health systems emphasize the importance of mobile-based technologies in improving communication between clients and healthcare providers. These technologies also enhance the management of care, as outlined in a Cochrane systematic review protocol published in 2018. 5. The WHO, in collaboration with the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the World Bank, published a report in 2018 titled Delivering Quality Health Services: A Global Imperative for Universal Health Coverage. This document underscores the need for quality healthcare services to achieve universal health coverage. 6. Moja L. and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2014, published in the American Journal of Public Health, to assess the effectiveness of computerized decision support systems linked to electronic health records. The findings demonstrate the potential of these systems to improve clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. 7. Agarwal S., Tamrat T., Glenton C., Lewin S., and others developed a Cochrane protocol in 2018 to evaluate the impact of mobile decision-support tools on the quality of care in primary healthcare settings. This protocol aims to assess the effectiveness of these tools in improving healthcare delivery. 8. Kawamoto K., Houlihan CA., Balas EA., and Lobach DF. conducted a systematic review in 2005, published in the BMJ, to identify critical features of clinical decision support systems that contribute to their success in improving clinical practice. 9. Bright TJ., Wong A., Dhurjati R., and colleagues performed a systematic review on the effects of clinical decision-support systems, as published in the Annals of Internal Medicine. The review highlights the potential benefits and limitations of these systems in healthcare settings. 10. Agarwal S., Vasudevan L., Tamrat T., Glenton C., Lewin S., and others developed a Cochrane protocol in 2018 to evaluate the use of digital tracking, provider decision-support systems, and targeted client communication via mobile devices to improve primary healthcare outcomes. 11. Tudor Car L., Riboli-Sasco EF., Marcano Belisario JS., and others published a Cochrane protocol in 2015 to assess the effectiveness of mobile learning in delivering health professional education. This protocol aims to evaluate the impact of mobile learning on healthcare workforce training. 12. The WHO's Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 outlines strategies to address global health workforce challenges. This document was accessed on November 25, 2018. 13. The introduction to HL7 standards, as provided by HL7 International, was accessed on March 7, 2019. These standards facilitate the exchange of electronic health information to improve healthcare delivery. 14. The WHO's International Classification of Diseases (ICD) provides a standardized framework for classifying diseases and health conditions. This resource was accessed on March 7, 2019. 15. The ISO website was accessed on March 7, 2019. 16. The RE-AIM framework, available on the RE-AIM website, provides a systematic approach to evaluating the impact of health interventions. 17. The Lives Saved Tool (LiST) is a resource for estimating the impact of health interventions on mortality and morbidity. This tool was accessed on November 22, 2018. 18. Lewin S., Hendry M., Chandler J., Oxman AD., Michie S., Shepperd S., and others developed the iCAT_SR tool to assess the complexity of interventions within systematic reviews. This tool was published in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2017. 19. The WHO's Digital Health and Interoperability Working Group, part of the Health Data Collaborative, focuses on advancing digital health solutions for sustainable development. This initiative was accessed on November 21, 2018. 20. The WHO and PATH are developing a planning and costing guide for digital health interventions in health programs. This forthcoming guide aims to support the implementation of cost-effective digital health solutions. 21. The WHO's website on innovation highlights the role of digital health technologies in addressing global health challenges. This resource was accessed on November 26, 2018. 22. The WHO guidelines on digital health interventions provide a shared language to describe the use of digital technologies in healthcare. These guidelines address various health system challenges, including loss to follow-up, data access, and resource allocation. 23. The guidelines also emphasize the importance of targeted client communication, decision-support tools, and digital tracking systems in improving healthcare outcomes for specific populations, such as adolescents, pregnant women, and children under five years of age. 24. The WHO's technical team and systematic review team, comprising experts from various institutions, contributed to the development of these guidelines. 25. The WHO steering group, including representatives from WHO headquarters and regional offices, provided oversight and guidance for the development of the digital health guidelines. 26. These declarations are summarized in the annex of the guidelines. 27. Evidence maps and illustrative research questions in the guidelines highlight trends in the effectiveness of digital health interventions. These maps demonstrate the need for rigorous research to address gaps in evidence and inform future recommendations.
